opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think "can LLMs reason?" is a question that tends to generate more heat than light, because people mean very different things by "reasoning." If by reasoning you mean the ability to retrieve and apply a memorized program, say, a template for solving a certain class of math word problem, then sure, LLMs can do that, and they can do it quite well. They've seen millions of examples of reasoning patterns, and they can reapply those patterns to new inputs. In that sense you can say they "reason."

But that's not really the interesting question. The interesting question is: what happens when the model faces something genuinely new, a situation it has not seen before and for which it has no memorized template? Can it synthesize a new program on the fly from the building blocks it has, and adapt to that novelty? That's what intelligence actually is, in my view. Intelligence isn't skill; it's the efficiency with which you acquire new skills, especially in situations you couldn't have prepared for.

And when you look at it that way, you see that LLMs are mostly interpolative databases of programs. They're extremely good when the test distribution is close to the training distribution, and they degrade sharply when it isn't. You can see this with very simple perturbations: change the surface form of a well-known puzzle slightly, and the model often falls back to the memorized answer for the original version. That tells you it was fetching rather than reasoning from first principles.

So framing it as adaptation to novelty gives you something you can actually measure. That's why I built ARC the way I did: every task is designed to be novel, so you can't solve it by memorization alone; you have to adapt. And it also points to what's missing. Scaling up the training data increases the coverage of the database, which makes the system look more intelligent, but it doesn't change the fundamental ability to deal with the unknown. What matters is whether the system can do test-time adaptation: search, recombine, actually construct a solution it has never seen. That's the question that will tell us whether we're on the path to general intelligence, rather than arguing over the word "reasoning."

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs can apply memorized programs or templates to new inputs and reapply learned reasoning patterns.

r002.rationale: It says a model could synthesize or recombine a solution from existing building blocks, but does not describe forming a model of the novel task.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe forming reusable abstractions from recurring combinations of existing building blocks.

r004.rationale: It does not say newly formed abstractions become building blocks for later problem solving.

r005.rationale: It does not state that access to a higher-level abstraction reduces the steps needed for a similar problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the reasoning question is kind of a trap, honestly, because "reasoning" is a word that nobody has pinned down. If you ask ten people what reasoning means you'll get ten different answers, and most of them will be answers that an LLM can already satisfy in some narrow sense. You can give it a chain-of-thought prompt and it produces something that looks like a sequence of logical steps. Is that reasoning? Maybe. It depends entirely on your definition, and so the debate just goes in circles.

Adaptation to novelty is different because it's operational. You can measure it. The question is: when you show the system something it has not seen before, something that is genuinely outside the distribution of its training data, can it figure it out? Can it synthesize a new approach on the fly, using what it knows, to solve a problem it has never encountered? That, to me, is what intelligence actually is. Intelligence is not a collection of skills. It's not knowledge. It's the efficiency with which you can turn your experience into new skills, in new situations, at test time.

And when you look at LLMs through that lens, the picture becomes much clearer. These models are extremely good at retrieving and recombining patterns they have memorized. They've seen an enormous amount of the internet, so for most tasks you can think of, there's something in there that's close enough. That gives the illusion of general reasoning. But if you construct a task that is simple for a human, something a child could do, but that doesn't resemble anything in the training data, performance collapses. That's what ARC was designed to expose, and for years it did exactly that.

So the reason I focus on novelty is that it's the thing that actually matters for whether you have a system that can operate in the real world. The real world is not a static dataset. It's constantly throwing situations at you that nobody anticipated. A system that can only handle what it's seen before, or minor variations of it, is a database with a nice interface. It's useful, I'm not saying it isn't, but it's not on the path to general intelligence. The capacity to adapt is the whole game, and it's the thing we still don't know how to build well. So that's the question I think is worth asking.

astra-6.text:
Well, because “reasoning” is a somewhat ambiguous term. You can look at a model producing a sequence of logical steps and say, okay, it’s reasoning. But that doesn’t tell you whether it’s applying a procedure it has seen many times before or actually figuring out how to deal with a new situation. The same observable behavior could result from very different processes.

For me, the central question is: can you adapt to something you weren’t prepared for? Can you take the knowledge you have and recombine it to solve a problem that requires something beyond rehearsing a familiar solution? That’s what makes intelligence useful. You don’t always know in advance what problems you’re going to encounter.

With LLMs, this distinction is particularly difficult to assess because their training data covers such an enormous range of situations. Something can be new to you, or even be a newly written question, while still being an instance of a very familiar pattern for the model. So success on a difficult question doesn’t necessarily demonstrate adaptation to novelty.

Reasoning is certainly relevant. But rather than arguing over whether a particular output qualifies as reasoning, I’d ask what happens when you move beyond the patterns the system was trained on. How efficiently can it learn something new? How much help does it need? Those are more concrete questions, and they get closer to what we actually want to understand about intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because “reasoning” is a very ambiguous word. You can observe a system producing the steps of a logical argument, but that doesn’t tell you how it acquired the ability to produce those steps. It might be applying a reusable abstraction, or it might be reproducing a pattern that was extensively represented in its training data. The output alone doesn’t settle that question.

What I care about is whether a system can deal with a problem that it wasn’t prepared for specifically. Can it take what it already knows and recombine it to acquire a new skill, given very little information? That’s the distinction between possessing skills and possessing the ability to acquire skills.

With LLMs, this is particularly difficult to disentangle because the training data is so vast. Something can look novel to you, as the person asking the question, while being very close to something the model has encountered during training. So success on a reasoning benchmark doesn’t necessarily establish the kind of generalization you think it establishes.

Adaptation to novelty gives us a more concrete question: what is new for the system, what prior knowledge does it have, and how much experience does it need to become competent? That gets much closer to what we actually want to understand about intelligence.
